newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-World Bank says China needs more revenue.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-World Bank says China needs more revenue.

text.p: China needs to increase government revenues substantially to meet pressing spending needs, the director of the World Bank's China and Mongolia department said on Wednesday.

"By our estimate, China needs an increase in government revenues of about six percent of GDP (gross domestic product), which would permit the covering of the existing deficit and provide an extra cover of four or five percent of GDP for investment in essential services," Nicholas Hope told Reuters in an interview.
Hope said China's massive tax reform of 1994 would help in time to fill government coffers, but in the interim government revenue and expenditure levels remain far apart.
Weakness in the government's financial situation "is one of the areas that the World Bank has pointed to as a chief constraint on China's ability to reform its macro economy quickly," said Hope.
Fiscal difficulties were also delaying reform of the state sector, he said.

"It is very difficult for the government to take on the social obligations of many of these enterprises, and until methods can be found for the government to take care of workers and retirees that would likely be displaced under comprehensive enterprise reform, the government is going to proceed very cautiously," Hope said.
World Bank lending to China hit US$3 billion in 1993 and would stay at that level through fiscal 1996, Hope said. Little change was expected in fiscal 1997, he said.
"We are planning a programme of about US$3 billion in fiscal 1997 and I don't anticipate that we would increase substantially from that level," he said.

The World Bank has been gradually decreasing loans to China through its concessionary IDA (International Development Association) fund, replacing these with market rate funding through the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD).
IDA funding generally is reserved for the poorest recipients. As countries grow richer, the World Bank typically reduces or eliminates concessionarly funding.
